When Mrs. Padma and her husband, Prakash mulled the idea of a new street food enterprise in the throes of the pandemic to stay afloat, they thought it would be unique to introduce the pizza but in a flavourful avatar that would resonate the punchy flavours that people expect in street fare. And thus was born Amma’s Italian Pizza, first on a cart and now a van. Padma Amma experimented with vegetarian topping combinations for days on end at her home, also sharpening her secret recipe for a piquant pizza sauce, a sprightly medley of herbs, spices, sour, sweet and heat. The name may say ‘Italian’, but these are the sort of pizzas that resonate the ‘kadak’, street vibes of namma ooru, Bengaluru.

After picking up recipes from a stint in a Maratha military hotel kitchen in Bengaluru, Rajanna, a native of Kunigal, began serving non vegetarian meals in a small shed off Magadi Road in Vijayanagar 36 years ago. The menu comprised only nine items, mostly mutton, cooked by Rajanna himself with a single masala that would be ground by him at home. He passed on shortly after, but his wife and brother in law have continued his work over decades, preserving the flavour and character of the food. From a shed, it is now a tiny eatery, sans any name board, where customers queue up for rustic, village style fare served on banana leaves off granite slabs that serve as benches and tables. A recent addition also includes a basic but functional family room. I caught up with my chef friend, Sushil Dwarkanath to explore the cooking here and also make a tasty meal of their mutton delicacies. If you love meaty, rustic flavours, this is the place to savour it.

When Gautham Reddy, a DJ, and his wife, Christine, a pastry chef, suddenly found themselves out of work due to the pandemic, they put together their savings into a culinary enterprise, a café, that met with limited success. Lesson learnt, they turned next to a home delivery business focused on non vegetarian fare derived from family recipes. Orders followed, giving them the confidence to set up a tiny eatery in the suburb of Vidyaranyapura. Things have been slow though, and when they reached out to us to help spread the word, we stepped in for a surprise visit one Wednesday afternoon. Manned by an all-women team, the fare here is the sort that is homely, tasty and most importantly, honestly priced. We tasted around 10 dishes, the sort that would happily feed a hungry party of four, and worked up a bill of just over Rs. 1200. I hope you have the heart to support enterprises like these that are committed to honest work, and trying to do their best to stay afloat in these trying times.

Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Over 30 years ago, Dinesh Sood and his brother Deepak Sood, originally from Ludhiana, set up a tiny four-table eatery in the old market area of Balepet, Bengaluru to serve North Indian khaana to traders and travellers who would visit the area. Gaining popularity over time, Punjabi Pure Veg moved to a slightly larger first floor nook eventually, where it still stands 28 years on. The ambience, service and the decor is rather basic, but it is the rustic flavours of the food dished out by second generation owner, Aman Sood and his motley retinue of cooks that seems to hold sway over regular patrons. Also, the fact that the fare is delightfully cheap further adds to its draw. Hope you enjoy this one, visit here only for the food, nothing else.

A couple of years ago, I had visited Kumar, a trained chef, who had turned his passion for omelets into an interesting enterprise, Egg Factor, where he would dish up gourmet ‘eggy’ creations out of a tiny stall in HSR Layout, South Bengaluru. Soon after the video was released, customers turned up in plenty to support him and it looked like nothing could go wrong. Until he arrived one morning to find his streetside eatery demolished without notice, and to make matters worse, the pandemic followed soon after. Today, Kumar and his wife, Rajalakshmi are once again trying to rebuild their lives and their small omelet  business with a borrowed push cart that is parked outside a supportive store. Hope you enjoy this episode. Do try your best to support fledgling businesses like this that are going through tough times. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!


Note: each omelet is made of four eggs and can easily serve two, or perhaps even three people with modest appetites. Please keep this in mind when considering prices here.

We stumbled into this tiny home eatery in Mudigere run by a young couple, Ravi and Vidya Pujari who began this to supplement their marginal coffee growing income. The food is Mangalorean, revolving around seafood that is procured fresh. We landed on the second Saturday of a month, a day when they supposedly don’t have too many customers and therefore do not procure a large variety of seafood. But what we tasted was the sort that was satisfying enough. The fries may have been slightly overdone, but was tasty nonetheless and the curries the sort that hit the spot along with a pleasing crab ghee roast. What’s nice overall is the warming hospitality with which the couple serve you in their modest eatery. Definitely a lunch spot to try should you be in and around Mudigere in Karnataka. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Sandeep Bhosle had to give up his gaddo (cart) a couple of years ago and move to a tiny stall on Dr Atmaram Borkar road in Panjim. But that hasn’t diminished the popularity of his ros omelet in any manner whatsoever. When the lights in his shop come on, the street food scene here comes alive. Dining off tables and stools arranged on the sidewalk, Sandeep’s clientele is a democratic mix of Goa, from the elite to the daily wage earners, for whom a plate of his xacuti gravy laden egg dish is bliss and the sort that Sandeep says,  “guarantees a good night's sleep.” Hope you enjoy this street food episode. Eshwar Rao entered the kitchen of a generations-old military hotel when he was barely into his teens. It was here that he learnt age-old Karnataka-Maratha recipes from his mentor, Rukmini Bai over decades of diligent labor, that he now serves up in his rustic eatery, S G Rao’s Military Hotel in Cottonpet, Bengaluru. I met this entrepreneur, now in his forties, and caught the making of a unique military style pulav, in addition to a tasting of some of the other must-haves here. The pulav here is cooked only with the gravy of the meat, the meat that is then layered under the rice just before serving. And interestingly, the chicken pulav too is cooked in any mutton gravy that may be available! Hope you enjoy this tasty episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

kesaramadu tumkur idli hotel, gangadhar idli hotel kesaramadu, tumkur, ghee roast idli, thatte idli, mini masala dosae,  tumkur kesarmadu hotel, kesaramadu roasted idli, kyathasandra, bangalore highway, nh 48, highway restaurant, bengaluru davanagere highway, idli, vegetarian, village breakfast, breakfast, snack, karnataka, support local, support small business

Gangadhar, real name Krishnamurthy, is a man who wears many hats - former president of the gram panchayat, farmer and eatery owner. It is the last hat though that is relevant here. 16 years ago, he set up a makeshift shed to serve the famous Kyathasandra thatte Idli but away from the bustle of the main Tumkur highway, on a narrow village road leading to a tiny hamlet, Kesaramadu. Slowly but surely the popularity of his solitary village eatery grew for its thatte Idli, dosae and simple rustic lunch that came as a boon to the farming folks around. However, four years ago some customers recommended that he try roasting the Idli in ghee, and thus was born his, now-referred-to-as, Kesaramadu Roast Idli. Thatte idlis are steamed, cooled and then slow roasted on a dosae tawa with liberal lashings of ghee. Ten minutes later, the idlis take on a delicious, buttery crust that sends the palate into raptures brought on by molten streams of ghee. And it is this idli that seems to have put Gangadhar Idli Hotel, Kesaramadu, on the food lovers map! Hope you enjoy this rustic breakfast episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Armed with an MBA, Harini wanted to get into the restaurant business with a concept that would serve tasty fare built on quality ingredients but at a price point that would not have pinched her purse as a student. Despite facing initial resistance to the idea from her father, she persisted, and finally after convincing her family for over six months, Zamindar Restaurant finally opened in HRBR Layout, East Bengaluru, with a menu repertoire that paid homage to her Andhra roots, biryanis, and spanning other cuisine influences to cater to Bengaluru’s cosmopolitan diners. In a relatively short span of under four years, her restaurant has carved out a significant niche for itself with its offerings that are built around the promise of “tasty fare at prices that offer maximum value”. I step into Zamindar for lunch, to meet her and her family who now support her enterprise unflinchingly and also taste some of the signature biryanis like the Hyderabadi biryani, ulavacharu biryani, gongura biryani, and other dishes that are a hit with customers. A trained pastry chef by profession, Kennedy Dias worked many years overseas crafting fine cakes and pastries. However, he yearned to be back home in Caranzalem, Goa. He finally returned and mustered the courage to set up a cake shop but “people didn’t understand fine pastries 20 years ago”, he says. So, after a couple of unsuccessful years, he began making puffs, pies and chops, the sort of traditional fare that locals appreciate and love. And along the way experimented with a home-smoked curry-leaf infused Goan sausage, that is now a must-try here. Since then, his tiny shop has become much popular with the locals and young students for his omelets, sandwiches, burgers, pies and interesting shakes and juices. This is the sort of honest dive that one should also visit for a true taste of small town Goa, away from the tourist trail.

Located in the heart of Panjim, Kokni Kanteen seeks to introduce guests to the Kokni, or traditional Saraswat cuisine of Goa,  in a format that is friendly and comfortable. Fitting when one learns that the bungalow it is housed in dates back to Portuguese rule and served as an inn where locals would be fed when they traveled from the villages. I step in here to savour a reasonably priced viswon (kingfish) thali and an interesting array of flavourful GSB preparations, both vegetarian and non vegetarian, that are rarely found outside homes. What began as a local haunt has now evolved to a destination where visitors can help themselves to a delicious serving of Goa’s rich and varied cuisines. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating.

Title: Must Stop Here For Famous Kadak Rotti, Enne Khara, Sappey Mutton! Hotel Nartaki Ranebennur Karnataka
Description:

enne khaara mutton, chicken, hotel nartaki, family run eatery, ranebennur, sappey mutton, chicken sukka, mutton chops, boti, khuska, non vegetarian eatery, north karnataka, highway eatery, karnataka food tour, north karnataka food tour, karnataka tourism, north karnataka cuisine, support local

I had heard much about this very special Ranebennur mutton preparation, the enne  khara, translating literally to oil and chilli heat, drawing from its two principal ingredients. And so on our recent drive to Goa, we planned a lunch stop in this agricultural town in North Karnataka at Hotel Nartaki, the home of this iconic dish. Established 30 years ago by N Satish, a tailor turned restaurateur, in a tiny eatery that could only accommodate a few customers at a time. His wife would help him make the masala at home that he would cook into curries. Along the way, he came up with the concept of enne khaara largely to appease the spice-hungry tastebuds of the locals. The dish, in contrast to its fiery name, is a beautiful balance of flavours between the chilli heat (from a combination of 90% local Javannur chillies that also impart a striking colour to the dish, and 10% Guntur chillies) and the oil that rounds off all the sharp edges of the masala aided by the sourness of tomatoes. Mr N Satish has since passed on but the homemade tradition continues with his sons, Chetan and Chandan, in a much larger space today, aided by their mother and wives. If you love your meaty fare, Hotel Nartaki is certainly worth a visit, I would say even a detour should you be travelling in the area. I hope you enjoy this very special episode. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

But when we arrived, the chicken xacuti was over as were some other popular breakfast eats like egg chops, etc.. Nonetheless, we stepped into the kitchen to check what was available and found the remnants of a xacuti gravy that owner, Mahesh Parsekar’s mother prepares at home. The roasted spice aroma of the gravy was enticing, and so when Mahesh offered to cook a ros omelet with the gravy, I knew we had to try it. The weighty omelet was elevated a few notches by the aromatic flavours of the xacuti, and I definitely look forward to returning to Sai Anant Parra someday in the hope of tasting more of the traditional home cooked fare. Hope you enjoy this short vlog on a hidden Goa gem. Happy eating; take care, stay safe and strong.

Run by the D'Souza family, the food here is the sort that you would taste in a Goan home if they were blessed with an extraordinary cook. The flavours are punchy and the hospitality of the family, warming, and the sort that immerses one in the conviviality of Goa’s people. A reason why this charming home eatery has endeared itself to locals and travellers for over 25 years. An acclaimed Yakshagana artist, Prabhakara Upadhyay began Saligrama’s Mantap Ice Cream in Bengaluru in 1981 when he realized the need for a business to earn a livelihood. In those days, the denizens of (then) chilly Bangalore were hesitant to eat ice creams afraid they may fall ill, and thus began a long and arduous journey of educating people to appreciate and enjoy these frozen treats. The effort seems to have paid off over the years, making this vegetarian ice cream parlour a household name amongst old Bangaloreans. From multiple outlets, Mantap has now scaled back to only one store in Seshadripuram, where Mantapa Upadhyay, (as he is popularly known) dreams up combinations that he personally puts together each morning with dairy rich ice creams that are sourced from a premium ice cream supplier. In this conversation with him and his family, I savour a range of his delectable creations - from traditional pure organic jaggery, guava chilli, to inspirations like the fruit fusion, red velvet cake, and classics like rich mango cream and caramel, and a couple of delicious faloodas too. This store is a definite must-visit if you love ice cream.

46 years ago, Rohidas Desai took over an existing taverna off Eduarte Pacheco street in Panjim to set up his seafood restaurant. Fastidious about the quality of seafood, he would visit the market each day to scour for the best marine produce to be cooked to his wife, Gokula Desai’s recipes. It is no surprise then that this committed approach had earned for Ritz legions of ardent patrons who now pack the group's six restaurants for lunch and dinner. I caught up with Daad (as he is known to everyone in Goa) Desai in a meeting that was ordained by destiny over a seafood lunch at their very first eatery, Café Ritz. Title: Is This Jayanagar’s Oldest Bajji Bonda Cart? 42 Years KUNDAPURA BONDA BAJJI SHOP, Bengaluru
Description:
#streetfood #jayanagar #bangalore

popular bajji shop in jayanagar, south bangalore, vegetable, pakora, bonda, capsicum masala bajji, aloo bonda, potato, mirchi bajji, street food, jayanagar, 4th block jayanagar, jayanagar street food, bengaluru, vegetarian eatery, bangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

Krishna Poojary migrated from his hometown in Kundapura to Bengaluru nearly half a century ago in search of a livelihood. After a string of odd jobs in eateries, he decided to try his hand at a bajji (fried fritter) gaadi (cart) in Jayanagar 4th block, Bengaluru. It’s been 42 years since; the location of his cart has changed from one street to another over the years, but the place that his fried wares occupy in the hearts and palates of his neighbourhood patrons remains constant to this day. Also perhaps making Kundapura Bonda Bajji Shop one of the area's oldest street food carts! I visited him one cloudy Bengaluru evening to taste all the bondas and bajjis he and his son have on offer. 

Hope you enjoy this episode in our ongoing initiative to support small businesses, do support your neighbourhood eateries too. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

On my last drive through the Western ghats into Mangalore, I stopped for lunch in the spice town of Mudigere, around 80 kilometres from Hassan, at an old bungalow converted into a cosy eatery. It was here that I met an incredibly hard working brother-sister duo. Kaleel makes a 240 kilometer return trip every other night to procure fresh seafood from the fishing harbour in Mangalore, that his sister Arshia single handedly cooks to family recipes. The flavours of the homely fare here is reminiscent of what you would taste in kudla (Mangalore)  but with the sort of punchy spicing that they say “is suited to the local palate of Mudigere”. Title: Traditional Village Style Kolhapuri Misal Cooked On Wood Fire At GAVRAN MISAL, Bengaluru
Description:
#misalpav #gavranmisal #bangalore

gavran misal, hsr layout, bengaluru, south bengaluru, authentic misal pav, kolhapuri misal, vada pav, rural, maharashtrian cuisine, street food, vegetarian snacks,  gavran misal recipe, gavran misal cooking, vegetarian eatery, bengaluru, bangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

Sujit Lakade missed Kolhapuri Misal Pav when he moved to Bengaluru a few years ago. In this he saw an opportunity to showcase to Bengaluru the village rendition of this quintessential Maharashtrian street food staple, an approach that conveys delicious, spicy flavours with minimal fuss. And so Gavran Misal was born, with ingredients sourced from Kolhapur, given his family’s lineage in the food grains business. Here, the tari, the spicy rasa (gravy) at the heart of the dish, is cooked over a wood fire, thereby also imbuing this modest eatery, with a rustic smokey appeal, where regulars wolf down the misal pav and vada pav, the only two items served here in addition to kokum and taak (buttermilk) to wash things down. 

If you’re looking to savour some authentic rural flavours, head here. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

When Mr Chenna Reddy migrated from his village in Andhra Pradesh just past the Karnataka border town of Mulbagal in the eighties, he sought employment as a cook in an Andhra eatery in Bengaluru. Such was his impressive hand at cooking, that some of his customers and associates pooled together a restaurant for him, and thus was born Mayuri in 1986, just off Minerva circle on JC Road. 36 years on, the eatery still reigns supreme for its Andhra fare, notably the vegetarian bhojanam and toothsome biryanis, the latter made to a unique recipe that employs minimal spices yet makes a terrific impact on the palate! In this episode, I catch up with Mr. Reddy as he walks me through his kitchen and preparations, his unbridled passion quite inspiring, before sitting down for a big Andhra meal comprising Mayuri’s most popular hits. Hope you find this slightly lengthy episode enjoyable, well, I certainly did 😉😋. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Title: Taste These Old World, Rare Breakfast Dishes at SRI RAM BHAVAN, Ayodhya Hotel, Mangalore
Description:
#srirambhavan #ayodhyahotel #mangalore 

sri ram bhavan restaurant, vegetarian, ayodhya  hotel mangalore, popular vegetarian restaurant, mangalore, south canara, dakshina kannada, patholi, patrode, thekrey idli, sanna polo, goli baje, neyyappam, biscuit roti, jackfruit roast, jackfruit halwa, jaggery jilebi, coconut barfi, coffee, 70 year old restaurant, mangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local

Stepping into Sri Ram Bhavan at Ayodhya Hotel is akin to stepping back in time. Not just in terms of its decor but the dishes that are served here, many which are found rarely now, and that too mostly in homes that have managed to hold on to their culinary traditions. I drop in for breakfast and and make a big breakfast of many delicacies that I hadn’t tasted hitherto - like the patholi, a stuffed rice and jackfruit pancake steamed in banana leaf, thekre idli, an unusual steamed rice dumpling made with cucumber, a raw jackfruit roast, patrode, spiced and steamed colocasia leaves, and lots more. If you want to savour an old-fashioned South Canara breakfast, more specifically a GSB meal, this is the place to visit when in Mangalore. Hope you enjoy this episode. Dating back to 1932, Sri Mahalasa Appu Shet Shop diversified into cooking egg based dishes around three decades ago. Creations like egg stumbler, a spicy assemblage of scrambled eggs, seasoned and toasted bread dices, a moist egg roll, among others have since made it a delicious habit for the denizens of Mangalore. And what better way to cool off, both from the weather, and spicy heat, than with some seasonal fruit juices and refreshing concoctions. I visited this store, now run by the third and fourth generation of the Shet family, one warm evening to make a big meal of a couple of egg snacks, a few fruit juices and a platter of fresh fruit. Appu Shet angadi certainly merits a visit when in this port city. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Title: Help Rescue This Brave Lady’s Food Truck! HALLI MANE ROTTIS Mangalore, Delicious Malenadu Cuisine!

halli mane rottis, food truck, mangalore, lady entrepreneur, shilpa, halli mane rotti shilpa, malenadu cuisine, manguluru, south canara, akki rotti, chicken green curry, palav, leg piece, halli mane rotti mangalore, mangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

During my very first Gourmet On The Road season over a couple of years ago, I visited this brave lady entrepreneur’s food truck, Halli Mane Rottis in Mangalore. Emerging through tough circumstances, her delicious Malenadu fare was winning hearts and palates in kudla and she seemed to be doing well, also winning numerous accolades for her grit and determination. However things are far from good for Shilpa and her family currently, I discovered when I chanced upon the food truck on my last visit to the city. I learnt that the family was going through a time due to the pandemic and also that Shilpa was largely confined to her home due to a serious back problem. She cooks what she can at home aided by her brother who then sells the food out of the truck with her father. Whilst their economic situation may be dire, the food that they dish out is still as delicious as before, I relished a toothsome green chicken curry, a spicy leg piece with soft akki rotti.

I hope you find it in your heart to support enterprises like Halli Mane Rottis. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Mr Balakrishna Prabhu and his wife, Sarojini began a tiny eatery in Kota, 60 years ago, then a little village enroute to Kundapur. Slowly but surely, the reputation of their tasty South Canara vegetarian fare cooked to family recipes grew not just with the support of locals, but travellers too for whom a visit to Hotel Latha was de rigueur after darshan at the famous Shri Amrutheshwari temple, located nearby. Today the second and third generation father and son duo of Venkatesh and Rajesh Prabu tend to this eatery’s affairs, overlooked by the matriarch of the house, Mrs. Prabhu. mamu idli hotel hassan, mamu idli hotel, 36 year old idli shop in hassan, mamu idli hassan, karnataka, spicy chutney, idlis, hyderabad dosa, dosae, breakfast stop in hassan, idli chutney, hassan food trail, karnataka, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

Mrs Prema continues in the legacy of her father, Mr Venkateshwara, who began a tiny idli hut in a bylane of Hassan adjoining the main market area. Over time the eatery moved to a tiny shop down the road, but its main offering, the idli continues to be a crowd pleaser, even 36 years on! Over 1500 of these are steamed each morning, to a unique batter that incorporates kusubalakki, urad dal and sabakki, sago pearls, in equal proportion; the Idlis are soft and sponge-like in texture to drink up the ghee that is drizzled over. It is served with a unique onion palya that is only tempered with salt and turmeric, and a fiery red chilli chutney made of peanuts, red chillies, cumin and garlic. The decor here is nothing to speak of, just some benches strewn around a tiny shed, but it doesn't seem to deter its patrons from lining up in queues to savour piping hot idlis for only the four or five hours they are open for business every morning.

In 1969, P. Ramachandra Upadhyay, then barely in his teens, migrated from Saligrama, Udupi district, to Kanakapura to work in Vasu Hotel, an eatery famous even then for its masala dosae. This form of the dosae though was a foreign concept to Ramachandra, who coincidentally came from a small village called Parampalli, where the khali dosa was prepared as an offering to Lord Maha Vishnu. Notwithstanding his lack of knowledge, the young lad worked hard in the kitchen and in a span of 14 years was handed ownership of the Vasu Hotel by the then owners who wished to retire. Nearly 50 years on, this no-frills eatery located 50 kilometers from Bengaluru still reigns supreme, not just for its sumptuous masala dosae and other old-fashioned tiffin and sweet treats, but also for its honest approach to pricing. I caught up with Mr Upadhyay and his son, Janardhan on a trip back from Mysuru.

Title: Best Traditional Karnataka Breakfast At KAMAT LOKARUCHI, Popular Mysuru Highway Eatery For 27 Years!
Description:

27 year old vegetarian eatery in ramanagara, popular mysore highway eatery, kamat lokaruchi, best traditional karnataka food, moode, neer dosae, chow chow bath, khara bath, kesari bath, breakfast, lunch, dinner, ramanagara, traditional meal, kamat lokaruchi ramanagara, kamat lokaruchi bangalore-mysore road karnataka, karnataka, karnataka food tour, support local

An eatery that began the Kamat Yatriniwas group’s foray into highway restaurants twenty seven years ago, Kamat Lokaruchi in Ramanagara serves the nourishing fare of rural Karnataka in an earthy atmosphere that seeks to connect diners to the land. Traditional staples are cooked over old fashioned stoves fuelled by wood to recreate authentic flavours of yore, the culinary philosophy employed here also shuns the use of artificial color and additives. Since they first opened doors, numerous eateries have mushroomed on the Mysuru highway, but even today, over quarter of a century later, Kamat Lokaruchi reigns supreme as one of the most popular eateries on the route. I caught up with Narayan Kamat, son of the late A. S. Kamat who established the Kamat Yatriniwas group, and also explored the kitchens and some wholesome dishes here. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Title: Softest Thatte Idli In Temple Town At 100-Yr-Old SUBBANNA MESS, Melukote | Must-Try Breakfast

During my lunch visit a few months ago to Subbanna Mess, a 100-year-old eatery in the temple town of Melukote in Karnataka, I happened to steal a glance at the preparation of the thatte idli batter, for breakfast the next morning. I was intrigued by the high proportion of urad dal as compared to typical idlis, and so made a mental note to return. And when we did, we were rewarded with tasting one of the softest idlis that I have ever eaten, in combination with a delicious, warming  cucumber gojju made. I also savoured their scrumptious no-onion masala dosae, again with an interesting twist, and their world-famous creations - puliyogare, bella pongal and sakkare pongal. This is a breakfast that I will gladly return to, and I hope this video makes your day too. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

When offered a free stall at the Mysuru Dussehra exhibition 27 years ago, Zainul Ahbideen felt he should in turn offer the city a taste of something different. And for his main ingredient, he chose the humble gobi, cauliflower, given the popularity of gobi manchurian, but in an avatar that had not been seen before. Experimenting with a spice mix he first made at home, Usman Dry Gobi emerged. It wasn't long before he moved to a street cart, and eventually a streetside stall a few years ago. Great care is taken by him and his son, Usman, to procure the right quality and size of cauliflowers, that are cleaned thoroughly and spiced with a secret masala, before being fried meticulously in a bath of hot oil. The result is the crunchiest, most flavourful dry gobi one can eat in Mysuru, and the sheer number of customers who queue up at this stall every evening stand testament to the fact that Usman’s Dry Gobi has emerged as one of this palace city’s most popular street food creations over the years. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

The Savaji community, settled for centuries in Karnataka, traces its ancestry to a race of warriors, originally from Maharashtra, and therefore it only seems natural that meat, especially mutton, forms an important part of their diet. 

Hotel Savaji’s Bengaluru pays allegiance to its owner, Narasingsa Kathare’s Savaji culinary roots, when he got into this business 25 years ago owing to circumstances, unable to find a job despite possessing an engineering degree and mba. He began his eatery cooking all dishes himself, wIth recipes gleaned subconsciously having watched his grandmother cook in his ancestral home in Hubli. Therefore, not surprisingly,  the flavours are the sort that one would find in a Savaji household in North Karnataka, the food cooked in a set up that quite resembles a home kitchen, not by professional chefs, but a small team of people who moved from Hubli to join Narasingsa. I step in here for a delicious meal of a sumptuous, mutton thali with the softest kaima unde, tasty chicken masala, mutton dry fry and other dishes. If you like your meaty preparations, albeit spicy, this is certainly a place to check out Savaji cuisine in Bengaluru.

This tiny eatery isnt easy to locate, hidden on the first floor of a nondescript building in a bylane of Rajajinagar. But once you ve eaten here, the flavors are the sort that will be permanently ‘landmarked’ on your palate. 

Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

When work brought Arpita and Sujoy Das to Bengaluru 13 years ago, they yearned for the flavours of Kolkata's street fare, more specifically the Calcutta kathi roll. Since they could find none, Arpita decided to open a tiny 150 square feet shop cooking and serving up this quintessential Kolkata eat-as-you-go treat. It was only a matter of time before Sujoy quit his advertising job to support this small enterprise that has since built for itself a loyal following not only for its rolls that are made completely in house, including the spice mix with a few ingredients shipped from Kolkata, but also their Kolkata style kebabs and biryani in recent times. I visit them for a late lunch and make a meal of three tasty kathi rolls.

Title: Making Of SREENIVASA BRAHMINS BAKERY Iconic CONGRESS KADLEKAI | Tasting KBC, Capsicum Puff, PalyaBun
Description:

popular bakery, traditional bakery, pure vegetarian bakery, bengaluru, basavanagudi, sreenivasa brahmins bakery, sreenivasa brahmins bakery bangalore, congress kadlekai, bread, kbc, khara bun butter congress, khara bun, palya bun, capsicum puff, nippat, bun butter jam, aloo bun, honey cake, gourmet on the road, kripal amanna, food lovers tv, food lovers india, truth in food

HR Ramaswamy Iyengar came to Bengaluru from Holenarsipur in 1956 and set up a bakery in Basavanagudi, an old market area surrounded by villages where groundnuts were cultivated. Selling a limited variety of pure vegetarian breads, buns and biscuits, the bakery fell upon hard times due to the rationing of flour and other essentials in the seventies. Faced with dire prospects, Ramaswamy Iyengar looked at the plentiful groundnut for survival and in doing so hit upon a unique recipe combining peanuts with a blend of spices that he named the Congress kadlekai, owing to the legend that during British times, secret notes were sent by Indian National Congress party workers hidden in sacks of groundnuts. I spent an afternoon with the second and third generation of the Sreenivasa Brahmins Bakery family to watch the making of the iconic Congress kadlekai and also taste some of the traditional items that make this 66-year-old institution a hit not just with locals, but also with Bengaluru diaspora across the globe who throng here for the kadlekai, nippat, khara buns, palya buns, puffs and other traditional Iyengar bakery treats.

Title: He Quit His Job For His Love Of Momos! Freshest Momos At MOMO SHOP, Bengaluru!
Description:
#momoshop #momos #bangalore 

neighbourhood momo shop, vegetable momo, mushroom momo, paneer momo, chicken momo, wholewheat momo, fresh momo, street food, bengaluru, bangalore, local, small business, local business, inspiring story, gourmet on the road, kripal amanna, food lovers tv, food lovers india, truth in food

In our continuing initiative to support small businesses, we visit Momo Shop, a passion enterprise of Ronald George who fell in love with momos whilst pursuing an advanced mountaineering course in Darjeeling, with plans to eventually join the army like his father and brother, both war heroes. Unfortunately, that wasn’t to be owing to an accident, necessitating him to switch tracks to a corporate career. However, after 11 years, he decided to return to his love for momos in 2010 and set up a tiny 100 sq. ft. shop in RT Nagar, North Bengaluru to serve the freshest momos. How fresh? Unlike typical momo shops which pre-cook and reheat momos to serve customers instantly, out here these steamed dumplings are prepared from scratch, from rolling out the dough to preparing the filling, only when an order is placed. This approach has won for Ronald a steady stream of customers over the years, facilitating his shop’s move to a slightly larger space. Hope you enjoy this episode enough to support neighbourhood eateries like the Momo Shop. Take care; stay safe and strong.

OG Variar & Sons Bakery, popularly known as Variar Bakery, traces its roots to 1954 when O Govinda Variar, a native of Kannur, Kerala, set up a small bakery in Guttahalli, Northwest Bengaluru, selling breads and buns. Eventually he moved to Rajajinagar in 1970 before opening a second bakery on Chord Road, West Bengaluru. What makes Variar bakery immensely popular with locals is its philosophy that “excludes artificial additives, preservatives and chemically bleached flour in its vast range of baked products.” As a result, “there is no shining in our items,” says second generation owner, Vijaya Shankar, who is currently on a quest to substitute, to the extent possible, detrimental fats with healthier options of unrefined oil, ghee, butter across most of their range, and in certain products, maida with wholewheat flour and grains. I spent the better part of a day exploring the bakery and tasting many of the must-haves at this institution that has spawned many imitators. A tiny village located atop the Charmadi ghat in Mudigere taluk of Karnataka, Kottigehara was a mere bus stop on this old route to Dakshina Kannada. Travellers would stop here for a few minutes and if hungry, would saunter off to one of the few home eateries on this remote, narrow strip of highway. And perhaps because its quick batter, water-like in its consistency, required almost no prep when an unexpected guest walked in, the neer dosae (neer meaning ‘water’ in kannada) quickly became the staple offering of this village centered around a bus stand. Whist many neer dosa stalls have mushroomed since, the oldest home eatery here is Anil Hotel, begun by Mrs. Mary 48 years ago and now managed by her son, Baby and his wife, Theresia. Famous for its honestly-priced homestyle curries, tasty preparations and warming hospitality that I first experienced a year ago, I learnt that the eatery was recently rebuilt after being demolished in highway expansion causing untold challenges to the family. In this episode, we revisit this tiny enterprise to not just savour their fare for the day but to also support them as they make a new beginning despite having a legacy of nearly half a century.

Say the word, ‘Pabba’s’ to anyone in Mangalore, or someone who has had the opportunity to visit this port city, and one is most likely to be met with a smile or in the very least, warming thoughts of  wistfulness. For very few, if at all any, in Kudla may have escaped to the alluring charm of the gadbad, tiramisu, parfait, bella candy and scores of other delicious ice cream creations concocted by S. Prabhakar Kamath, affectionately known as Pabba to family and friends, over half a century at his now iconic Mangalorean institution, Pabba’s and Ideal Ice Creams. On my visit to kudla nearly a couple of months ago, I had the opportunity to sit with him (after nearly 20 years), his son, Mukund, and grandson, Mohith, to taste their latest creation, the I. Thali, a tantalising ice cream take on the South Indian thali, at their newest parlour, Pabba’s Ideal Café, Bharath Mall, that seems to have taken Mangalore by storm going by the sheer numbers that queue outside this large restaurant. However little did I know then, that this would be my last meeting with him! This episode was conceived as a review of the I Thali, but is now in some ways a tribute to the man who put Mangalore and his legendary ice creams on the culinary map.

Native to Africa and Middle East, and imported first into the country decades ago as part of a food security programme, the tilapia, a rather productive species of fish, came to be known as jilapia in native tongues, eventually acquiring the moniker ‘jilebi’ meenu or fish. And the tiny village of Buyyanadoddi in Mandya district, 90 kilometres outside Bengaluru, is making ripples with food lovers for its “jilebi” fish fry. 

The fish is caught fresh from streams in the area, marinated and then tawa fried over a wood fire, slathered continuously with a spicy green chilli paste and liberal sprinklings of crushed pepper, in a clutch of home eateries here. And over the years, its appeal seems to be catching on not just with locals but also Bangaloreans looking for a tasty outing and to experience Buyyanadoddi’s rustic appeal.

Pandavapura, located on the state highway between Srirangapatna and Melukote in Mandya district of Karnataka, would perhaps not have registered as a breakfast stop on the traveller’s map, but for an idli shop that goes back over three decades. Actually, it isn’t even a shop, but a window in 60-something-year-old Shivappa’s home from where he dispenses freshly steamed idlis (only) with home churned butter for a few hours each morning. Travellers on the route, and even those who journey from afar just to eat here, line up outside the window, even before it is flung open at 7am.

Shivappa’s enterprise bears no signboard and he employs no one, preferring to do everything himself, from preparing the chutney and the butter to the soaking and grinding of the grain, the fermentation and steaming of the idlis, helped only by his wife. When you are here, you need to abide by his “seemingly authoritarian” rules - register your order, collect a token in exchange for your payment, and wait patiently for Shivappa to steam the idlis fresh and call your token number! This may seem like a bit of a drill, until you take a bite of the spicy chutney soaked idlis, and then it all seems to make sense. Like we discovered when we drove 130 kilometres from Bengaluru for breakfast recently. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and happy eating.

Description:

babusingh’s thakur pedha, famous dharwad pedha, original dharwad pedha, mithai, dharwad peda, dharwad, babusingh thakur pedha, hubli, hubbali, north karnataka food tour, dharwad food trail, dharwad food tour, hubli food trail, hubli food tour
 
There can be no mention made of Dharwad without its most renowned export, the Dharwad Pedha. Not many know this, but the original version made at Babusingh’s Thakur Dharwad Pedha has a legacy that goes back over 150 years when a halwai (sweetmeat cook), Ramratan Singh migrated to Karnataka from Unnao near Lucknow to escape the plague. A new beginning was made in Dharwad where he would roam the markets with a tray of unique pedha to sell. It was only a matter of time before the taste of this roasted khoya creation caught the fancy of local palates, and like they say, the rest is history. Generations later, the Dharwad Pedha may be shipped across the globe, but is still handmade the old-fashioned way. I met with Karan Singh, sixth generation of the Babusingh’s Thakur family to learn more about the making of this iconic Dharwad mithai. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care, stay safe and strong. Description:

belgaum’s most famous biryani, popular biryani restaurant in belgaum, niyaaz biryani belgaum, chicken biryani, mutton biryani, biryani making, belagavi, belgaum, belagavi biryani, niyaz belgaum biryani, niyaaz hotel belgaum biryani recipe, north karnataka food tour, belgaum food trail, belgaum food trail, belgaum food tour

How do biryanis become iconic? Well, most begin as tentative experiments and over a period of time endear themselves to the palate of the locals. So much so that the denizens of the place become vocal ambassadors for the biryani. And when it comes to Belagavi (Belgaum), the Niyaaz biryani is one such icon. Made in the kacchi akhni style, in which semi-cooked rice is layered over twice-marinated meat and cooked on dum, the Niyaaz biryani is subtle in its character, owing to a unique blend of spices, and the light fragrance of a short-grain locally grown rice that is used in combination with the more typical long grain basmati rice. What began as a family’s endeavour to create a unique biryani 30 years ago is now unarguably one of Belagavi’s most popular dishes. In this episode, I drive to Belgaum to meet co-owner, Niyaaz Abdussalam Saudagar, and explore in depth the making of both the chicken and mutton biryani, before proceeding to make a meal of these distinct Belagavi culinary signatures. Title: Her Culinary Tribute To Her Late Husband! AGRAANE KITCHEN Bengaluru | Street Food Of Hubli
Description:

In happier times, Bhagya Kulkarni’s conversations with her husband, noted television personality, Sanjeev Kulkarni, often revolved around bringing the street food of Hubballi, their hometown to Bengaluru. Their trips back home always included tasting forays to the eateries of Durgadbail and incessant recipe experimentations to perfect the robust masalas of Hubli street fare. When he fell ill, she set up a small business catering Uttara Karnataka meals out of their home in South Bengaluru to support the family. Unfortunately, he passed on, but Bhagya Kulkarni was determined to fulfil their dream, and thus was born Agraane Kitchen, a tiny shop that serves up the Durgadbail girmit, mirchi, avalakki usli, bun bonda, cut mirchi, etc., in addition to typical breakfast offerings and an austere but wholesome jowar rotti meal during lunch. I visit them on a rainy evening to savour the spicy, snacky street fare that I missed on my recent Hubli expedition, and to also support this enterprise that in a manner of speaking, is this brave lady’s culinary tribute to her late husband. Established in 1940, Suvarna Mandir is perhaps Hubballi’s oldest restaurant, if not the oldest. Located amidst the hustle and bustle of Durgadbail market, it’s quite easy to miss the tiny doorway that opens into a courtyard setting in an ancient home from nearly a century ago. Looked after by third generation custodian Mr. Prakash Bhatt, when asked if he was the owner, replied that he was merely taking care of the space like his grandfather and father had before him, this eatery’s charming old school disposition extends to the fare that is served here. Misal, aloo bonda, poori bhaji, madke kaalu, etc. typical Hubli vegetarian breakfast snack fare, but one that is steeped in nostalgia for the locals, and reminiscent of old-fashioned goodness if you happen to be a visitor like me. When it comes to the ubiquitous masala dosae here in Bengaluru, everyone has an opinion, actually many opinions, and clear favourites. Stuck at home during the recent lockdown, I couldn’t help but reminisce tasting three of Bengaluru’s most popular versions, and put together a special compilation for you, highlights of the CTR, MTR (Mavalli Tiffin Room, Lalbagh) and Vidyarthi Bhavan masala dosae from Gourmet On The Road.

Hope you enjoy this short and scrumptious bonus video; take care, stay safe and happy eating! 

CTR Benne Masala Dosa
This butter-drenched gold-hued dose is blessed with the perfect gentle crackle. On the palate, one tastes the lushness of the homemade butter that envelopes every bite of the dose, the palya and the chutney with its delicious veil. If you need one reason to visit CTR, this would be it.
Rs. 57 (usd 0.8)
10/10

MTR MASALA DOSA
The dosa here is iconic and never disappoints. Made with a blend of three rice varieties, including two red rice varieties that lend a toasty colour tone, the dose is crisp outside and soft within. The palya is seasoned just right. 
Rs. 90 (usd 1.3)
10

Vidyarthi Bhavan Masala Dosa
If you need one reason to visit Vidyarthji Bhavan, this would be it. A dose that’s crisp and lacey in parts, soft and fluffy in others, and hides within its single fold a creamy potato palya. The chutney is spicy and vivacious, a bold complement to the gentle flavours of the dose and palya.
Rs. 53 (usd 0.7) 
10/10

Nagajyothi and her husband Manish Eswar gave up successful careers in the corporate world to set up Bangalore Tiffins, a modest eatery in Jakkur, North Bengaluru, where they serve traditional vegetarian tiffin fare made to their family recipes. Their offering is endearing in its simplicity, keeping in line with this young couple’s philosophy of serving “food that is pure and devoid of artificial additives, like soda, colours and taste enhancers.” Notwithstanding the current situation, and many setbacks along the way, including one where they lost all their cooks, thereby compelling Nagajyothi to take charge of the kitchen, Bangalore Tiffins holds promise in building for itself a solid reputation on the basis of its food, especially dishes like the pudi idli and masala dosa that I tasted on this breakfast outing. Title: ANAND Dum Biryani Vs. MANI Dum Biryani! Which Famous HOSKOTE Early Morning BIRYANI Should You Try?
Description:
#hoskote #biryani #bangalore

mani dum biryani, anand dum biryani, popular hoskote biryani shop, early morning biryani, popular biryani shop,, hosakote, hoskote, bangalore, bengaluru, mutton biryani, biryani trail, inspiring stories, karnataka

The Hoskote early morning biryani draws hundreds of faithful fans who wake up at an unearthly hour every Tuesday, Friday and Sunday to make the 40-km trek to queue up at biryani shops in this town just outside Bengaluru. 

However, for those not completely in the know, some of the most commonly asked questions with respect to this long-standing biryani tradition are: What’s the fuss about the Hoskote biryani? Which biryani should one try, should one try the Mani Biryani or the Anand Biryani? How different are these biryanis? Or are they similar? Which one is spicy, which one is not? What goes into the making of these hugely popular biryanis? Which one came first? And more… 

In this special Gourmet On The Road episode, we revisit these biryanis and compare side by side Hoskote’s most popular early morning biryanis, undoubtedly, in an attempt to answer many of the questions posed. Hope you enjoy this one; take care, stay safe and happy eating! 

Anand Mutton Biryani 
The dominant flavours in this biryani are that of the fresh ingredients, the naati ginger, garlic, coriander,mint etc., followed by a veil of the aromatic spices. Every grain of rice is imbued with its flavours, and the meat is a combination of some soft, juicy pieces and some on the bone, that calls for a bit of effort to get to every bit of it, some fat included. The spicing is gentle and warm. 
Rs. 230 (usd 3.1) 
9/10

Mutton Biryani
The only dish made at Mani Dum Biryani, is unique in its aroma that is redolent of an amalgam of spices combined with meat. Each grain of the rice has absorbed the procession of spices that go into the pot and the fat that is rendered from the meat, this is the sort of biryani that leaves behind a spicy impression on the palate. You can taste the heat of green chillies, and the flavour of the secret spice mix that’s made in Mani’s home. Some of the meat is laced with fat that melts in the warmth of one’s mouth, some pieces though can have a bit of a bite. This is a spicy biryani, and the mosaru bhajji, onion and cucumber raitha helps cool things down.
Rs. 230 (usd 3.1)
9/10

Title: Bengaluru’s SOFTEST IDLIS Takeaway| BRAHMINS’ COFFEE BAR | Idli, Vada, Chowchow Bath | Rerun Episode
Description:
#brahminscoffeebar #idlivada #bangalore

support local eateries, takeaway south indian breakfast, brahmins’ coffee bar, idli, vada, chutney, kesari bath, khara bath, shankarapura, bangalore, bengaluru

When it comes to soft, melt-in-the mouth idlis, all roads lead to Brahmins’ Coffee Bar idlis, or at least it did until the current situation. I visit this modest South Bengaluru eatery that’s big on its reputation to see how they are coping with life post covid, and take back a parcel of their entire menu consisting of all of four items only! Are the idlis still as soft? Well, you’ll have to watch this one to find out. Stay safe and happy eating!

Note: This episode was first released in May 2020 and is being rerun to support Bengaluru eateries with takeaway orders in the current situation. Please support local eateries.

Takeaway Dish Review

Idli
A coarse-grained porous idli that allows for the chutney to seep in, you can taste a slight tartness from the fermentation. With the spicy ghatti chutney, that is made of hurukadale, roasted Bengal gram, coconut and  the idli takes on a bold, flavourful avatar. Pour the ‘telu’ or ‘flowy’ mint-coconut chutney over the idli to make for a bite that melts in the mouth.
Rs. 34 (usd 0.45) for 2 idlis 
 
Uddina Vade
It’s a tough act for the vade to follow the idli in takeaway mode, given that the vade is best savoured hot and crispy. However, a saving grace here is the vade is studded with curry leaves, green chillies, peppercorns, fresh coconut, thereby making for a flavourful bite. Soak up the past-warm vade with the chutney to relish the warming heat from the green chillies in the chutney. 
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3) per vade

Khara Bath
BCB’s khara bath is a flavourful one, embellished with curry leaves, toasted lentils, mustard seeds, grated coconut, coriander, tasty enough to be savoured sans the chutney. But if you like it spicy, go ahead and introduce it to the zesty gatti chutney. 
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3) 

Kesari Bath
End your takeaway tiffin with the kesari bath! There’s tonnes of ghee that goes into this sweet semolina and vermicelli concoction and you can taste it in its lush richness. The flavours draw from the tangy fruitiness of the pineapple and the warming cloves. The plum raisins add a sugary pop when you bite into one. 
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3) 

Note: I haven’t rated these as I feel it would be unfair to rate South Indian breakfast items in a takeaway format. Since this is a rerun episode, prices of the dishes may have changed since.

Title: CHAAT, North Indian veg Thali, Mithai Takeaway From BHARTIYA JALPAN 75-Year Legacy | Rerun Episode
Description:
#bhartiyajalpan #vegetarian #supportlocal

support local eateries, takeaway, bhartiya jalpan, chats, chaats, vegetarian thali, mithai, namkeen, samosa, chole bhature, dahi bhalla, aloo tikki, north indian, bangalore, bengaluru

To quell a chaat and north indian veg food craving, we take away from the Bengaluru outpost of Bhartiya Jalpan, a 75-year-old mithai and namkeen house from Guwahati, Assam. Now whilst takeaways aren’t the best way to savour desi chaats, we found the flavours spot on if you’re looking to savour some chatpata desi fare. Hope you enjoy this episode. Stay safe and happy eating.

Note: This episode was first released in June 2020 and is being rerun to support Bengaluru eateries with takeaway orders in the current situation. Please do support local eateries.

Samosa
The dark spiced stuffing makes this a chatpata samosa, the pastry is flakey and still retains its crunch despite being cold. The date chutney is warming and spicy.
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3) per samosa 
8.5/10

Chole Bhature
A popular snack at BJ, the bhatura loses its puffy vigour in takeaway mode, but is still redeemed by the deep flavours of the chole (chickpeas). Definitely a dish that needs to be snacked on when at the eatery as opposed to takeaway.
Rs. 150 (usd 2) 

Raj Kachori
The kachori had become soggy by the time we turned our attention to this yoghurt laden chaat, but the crisp sev and moth beans still offer crunch. The yoghurt is sweet, savoury and sour. 
Rs. 129 (usd 1.7) 

Dahi Bhalla
A dumpling (bhalla) made of rice flour and urad dal, topped with spiced yoghurt, this is the perfect takeaway chaat as the bhalla has soaked up the spicing from the yoghurt and the chutneys. 
Rs. 90 (usd 1.2) 
9/10

Aloo Tikki
A potato patty stuffed with a spice mix and shallow fried on a griddle until crisp, and served with peas gravy. Smash the patty along with the peas to help the chutneys seep into the potato.
Rs. 129 (usd 1.7) 

Bhartiya Jalpan Shaahi Thaali
A tray laden with paneer makhani, aloo mutter, daal, boondi raita, jeera rice, chapatis, a sweet, pickle and papad, this meal option is a sumptuous one. I found the chapatis soft, the paneer soft and creamy, the vegetables cooked the manner they should be and the dal a nourishing accompaniment to the jeera rice. 
Rs. 269 (usd 3.6) 
8/10

Malai Chamcham
The chamcham just dissolves in one’s mouth leaving behind a veil of aromatic sweetness. Highly recommended.
Rs. 38 (usd 0.5) 
9/10

Rabri
Sweetened milk braised slowly over hours and topped with thick cream and nuts, what’s there not to like!
Rs. 81 (usd 1.1) 
8.5/10

Title: Iconic MAVALLI TIFFIN ROOM Veg Lunch Evolves For Takeaway! Rava Idli, Masala Dosa |  Rerun Episode
Description:
#mtr #vegetarian #supportlocal

support local eateries, takeaway, mtr, mavalli tiffin rooms, lalbagh, vegetarian lunch, thaali, rava idli, masala dosa, hema malini maiya, bangalore, bengaluru

Step into Mavalli Tiffin Rooms, the city’s oldest eatery, In this throwback episode to see how they have evolved their popular 21-item traditional lunch to a more convenient and packaging-friendly 9-dish mini-meal. 

From revamped, sanitised processes to consolidated menus, this century-old institution is revamping and reworking processes to meet the needs of the current situation. But then, that shouldn’t come as a surprise, because after all, they do have a tradition of innovating through adversities in the past, as illustrated in the invention of the rava idli during the rice famine of the 40s, or the seed for MTR packaged foods that was sown during the 1975-77 emergency. 

Note: This episode was first released in May 2020 and is being rerun to support Bengaluru eateries with takeaway orders in the current situation. Please do support local eateries.

Mini Meals
No longer the enormous spread that would be a delicious gateway to a post-lunch slumber, the mini meals is compact in its post-covid avatar. But that doesnt get in the way of making for a satisfying lunch, puri, saagu, rice, rasam, palya, mosaru anna, poppadom, uppinakayi and payasam, the mini meal has all that you need to savour a taste of Mavalli Tiffin Room. 
Rs. 162 (usd 2.1) 
8/10

Masala Dose
Although packed in a foil-lined box, the masala dose is missing its crunch in takeaway mode, understandably, as opposed to when savoured at the restaurant. You can heat it on a tava with a dollop of ghee to make some amends, and the flavours are trademark MTR, the sprightly chutney smeared inside the dosa and the flavourful, bright aloogadde palya. The chutney is rich in coconut and green chilli spice. All in all, makes for a delicious takeaway dose, once you get past the expectation of eating something crisp.   
Rs. 90 (usd 1.2)

Rava Idli
A dish born of a crisis, the rava idli is said to have been invented in the kitchens of Mavalli Tiffin Rooms, when there was a shortage of rice during the famine of the 40s. This is a flavourful rava idli that is rich in yoghurt, embellished with coriander, mint, coconut and topped with toasted cashew, and does spectacularly well as a takeaway. The aloogadde sagu serves well to moisten the idli with its savoury character. 
Rs. 60 (usd 0.8)

Sharbath

Vegetarian Carrier Meals

Title: Tasting VIDYARTHI BHAVAN Bengaluru's Iconic MASALA DOSA In Lockdown Takeaway | Rerun Episode
Description:
#supportlocal #vidyarthibhavan #masala dosa

support local eateries, takeaway, vidyarthi bhavan, basavangudi, south bangalore, traditional vegetarian tiffin in bangalore, masala dosa, dose, idli vada, chutney, old world restaurant, traditional eatery, bangalore, bengaluru

In its 78 years of existence, Vidyarthi Bhavan has always served its iconic masala dose within its premises, keeping it strictly outside the purview of delivery services. However the current scenario calls for an entirely new approach in food service, and in keeping with this, this revered South Bengaluru eatery has embraced takeaway as a new way of life, at least for the foreseeable future. I visit Vidyarthi Bhavan to document this change from the past and see for myself how its management is taking all steps necessary to ensure continuity of its delicious culinary traditions in as safe a manner as possible. Hope you enjoy this episode. Stay safe and happy eating!
Note: This episode was first released in May 2020 and is being rerun to support Bengaluru eateries with takeaway orders in the current situation. Please do support local eateries.


Masala Dosa
The masala dose is now folded twice as opposed to the VB classic one fold, an allowance that the eatery has made for the dose to be rolled into an aluminium foil in order to retain its temperature when savoured at home. The crispy crackle of the dose is now replaced by a whisper of a crunch, but the buttery flavours are still spot on. The dose oozes ghee, and the aloogadde palya is mildly seasoned and creamy. It helps to crispen the dose a bit on the pan just before eating. 
Rs. 50 (usd 0.7) 

Idli
VB’s idlis are the grainy sort, perfect for ladling over chutney and piping hot sambar, before breaking it down to a delicious, spicy mash. If they’re too cold by the time they get to you, steam for a couple of minutes.
Rs. 26 (usd 0.3) 

Uddin Vade
The vade definitely suffers the most casualty when consumed in a takeaway format. Gone is its crisp crunch, that would yield to a porous bite. The only way to redeem the vada is to dunk it into a bowl of piping hot sambar and savour it with a dollop of spicy chutney.
Rs. 26 (usd 0.3) 

Khara Bath
The kharabath travels extremely well, given its moist texture. This tasty dish is studded with onions, fried lentils, coconut flakes and curry leaves, making for a playful medley of flavours and textures.
Rs. 26 (usd 0.3) 

Kesari Bath
End your meal with this luscious semolina preparation, the flavour of the pineapple and cloves is quite pronounced. The dish is mellow in its sweetness, save for the pop of extra sweetness when you bite into a toasted raisin.
Rs. 26 (usd 0.3)

Links to references I have looked up to determine if eating outside food is safe:

Specifically, coronaviruses are thermolabile, which means that they are susceptible to normal cooking temperatures (70°C). Therefore, as a general rule, the consumption of raw or undercooked animal products should be avoided. Raw meat, raw milk or raw animal organs should be handled with care to avoid cross-contamination with uncooked foods.
Source: WHO https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20200221-sitrep-32-covid-19.pdf

Food containers and packaging. There's no evidence of anyone contracting the virus that causes COVID-19 after touching food containers and food packaging. Many restaurants are now offering no-contact takeout and delivery to lessen the risk of transmission.

Still, if you're concerned, it's reasonable to follow general food safety guidelines. Wash your hands for at least 20 seconds with soap and water after handling takeout containers, and then transfer food to a clean dish using clean utensils. Wash your hands again before eating. After disposing of containers, clean and disinfect any surfaces that had takeout containers on them.
Source: Mayo Clinic, https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/coronavirus/expert-answers/can-coronavirus-spread-food-water/faq-20485479
Food Standards Australia & New Zealand, https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/safety/Pages/Can-COVID-19-be-transmitted-by-food-or-food-packaging.aspx

COVID-19 is a respiratory disease spreading from person to person. It’s not a foodborne disease. There’s no evidence to suggest people will get infected by swallowing the virus in, or on, food or drink.
Source: Food Standards Australia & New Zealand, https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/safety/Pages/Can-COVID-19-be-transmitted-by-food-or-food-packaging.aspx

Title: TARAYI COASTAL CUISINE | This Family Eatery Is A Labour Of Love! Fish Thali, Ghee Roast, Crab Masala
Description:
#seafood #mangalorean #bengaluru

family eatery, st thomas town, east bangalore, new restaurant, coastal cuisine, fish thali, fish fry, pomfret, mackerel, fish fry, prawn ghee roast, crab masala, chicken curry, small business

Tarayi, a tiny three-table eatery in St. Thomas Town, East Bengaluru, was born of homemaker Freeda Ananth’s desire to share the culinary legacy of her late mother and to set up a small business of her own. So, with the support of her husband, Vijay Ananth, this soft-spoken lady ventured out as a restaurateur just a couple of months ago, and in a relatively short span of time has managed to make an impression on the neighbourhood with her rendition of Mangalorean-Kundapur fare laced with a touch of Kerala influence. I visited Tarayi to taste their limited but tasty homestyle offerings, and to also help share the word on this family enterprise that’s a true labour of love. Hope you enjoy this episode, take care, stay safe and happy eating!

Prawn Ghee Roast
This ghee roast masala exudes a slight sour twang followed by the warmth of the chilli and spices. The prawns are cooked just right, delicately ‘springy’ on the bite, swaddled in the grainy textured masala with the lushness of ghee.  
Rs. 270 (usd 3.6)
9/10

Black Pomfret Fry 
The masala is napped rather lightly on the fish, allowing for the pomfret to shine in its fresh flavours. The skin is cooked to a perfect crisp.
Rs. 250 (usd 3.3)
8.5/10

Seer Fry
Rs. 280 (usd 3.7)
8/10

Crab Masala
Loved the aromatic masala, onions, tomatoes and spices, soaked up by the plump, meaty sea crab. The sweet crab meat contrasts beautifully with the savoury notes of the masala. If you love crab, this is certainly a must-order when here.
Rs. 240 (usd 3.2)
10/10

Fish Thali
A satisfying thali, complete with modest portions of mackerel curry and fry, in addition to sambar, rasam, vegetables, boiled rice… perfect if you’re looking to savour Mangalorean fare on a budget.
Rs. 150 (usd 2)
8/10

Kheema Ball Curry
A pleasing curry, I found the meat ball a tad pasty and giving up the texture of the flour used to bind the mince together.
Rs. 120 (usd 1.6) for half portion
7/10

Chicken Curry
A homestyle curry, thin in its consistency but rich in the flavour of the masala. Goes well with the neer dosae. 
7.5/10


Kripal Amanna,
Gourmet On The Road,
Food Lovers TV

Note: This is a tiny eatery with barely three tables; if dining here, be prepared for a bit of a wait. Best perhaps to order in, they are registered on Dunzo for now.

Description:
#biryani #streetfood #mysore

biryani food truck, nrk bamboo biryani, mysuru, bamboo biryani, mutton biryani, chicken biryani, chicken tawa fry, small business

On my last trip to Mysuru, I visited this food truck that cooks an unusual biryani, layered and steamed in bamboo. Helmed by a relatively new food entrepreneur, Ramamurthy, who was left with no option but to move to Mysuru and begin this mobile eatery to support his family after losing his life’s savings, the bamboo biryani is a result of his culinary passion and kitchen experiments. This version of the biryani that is steamed in bamboo for a couple of hours, isn’t what one may traditionally expect, but certainly makes for an interesting dish to taste! Check it out if you find yourself in Mysuru. Hope you enjoy this short and sweet episode, take care, stay safe and happy eating!

Mutton Biryani 
The sort of biryani that tumbles onto the plate when semi-cooked meat masala is placed in the bottom of a bamboo cylinder, topped with aromatic rice and egg,  and steamed for a couple of hours. The thick masala clinging to the meat serves to moisten the rice and the meat, some pieces soft and yet others that warrant a bit of a chew. The bamboo lends its aroma to the preparation.
Rs. 200 (usd 2.7)
7.5/10

Title: GANGA’S MUDDE MANE | Homely Gowda Cuisine| This Brave Couple Makes A Fresh Start Despite Challenges!
Description:
#traditional #gowdafood #bangalore

new gowda cuisine eatery, vegetarian thali, non veg meal, nalli fry, ragi mudde, kheema unde curry, mutton peas pulav, kaal soup, boti gojju, chicken tava roast, small business

A sudden loss of occupation forced Hemanth Kumar to deploy his life savings and rustle up an eatery to support his family. Seeing her husband struggle, Nalini gave up her teaching job to support him in this enterprise that aspires to serve homestyle Gowda food. I visited Ganga’s Mudde Mane one afternoon to meet and motivate the brave couple, and along the way tasted an elaborate spread. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and happy eating!

Kaal Soup 
An aromatic soup that serves well to whet your palate. The tomato conveys a pulpy texture laden with the meaty broth.
Rs. 40 (usd 0.6)
8/10

Brain Fry
Flavoured with the lightest touch of spice, pepper and curry leaves, the ‘bheja’ is cooked to perfection and melts in its rich buttery lushness when placed in the mouth. If you love the brain, a must-order here!
Rs. 150 (usd 2.1)
10/10

Chicken Tava Roast
Marinated in a green chilli, ginger garlic paste, it is the freshness of the mint that shines through the masala. I found the chicken a tad chewy. 
Rs. 190 (usd 2.6)
7.5/10

Boti Kal Goju 
A thick preparation enlivened with the starchiness of raw banana and nourishment of lentils, the boti is cooked through well. 
Rs. 170 (usd 2.3)
8/10

Mutton Kheema Ball Curry
The kheema unde is rich in its meatiness and is complemented by the green chilli and coriander. Eat this hot to prevent the gram flour, used to bind the meat, from making its presence felt on the palate.
Rs. 180 (usd 2.5)
7.5/10

Chicken Kheema Goju 
Tiny cubes of chicken tossed in a tasty masala. What makes this dish interesting are flecks of yam that bring its earthy flavours. 
Rs. 150 (usd 2.1)
7/10

Nalli Fry 
A weighty lamb shank, some of the meat has a bit of a bite, but as you work your way to the core of the nalli, the meat is tender. There is depth of flavour from the spices and the pepper. 
Rs. 380 (usd 5.2) for two large pieces, the price for this varies by weight. 
9/10

Veg Meals 
A vegetarian will enjoy this simple but homely assemblage with as much gusto as a non vegetarian. From the scrumptious dill fritters to the comforting sprouts saaru and rasam, each dish bears the mark of a talented home cook, in this case, Nalini Hemant Kumar. I would happily order this with a non-vegetarian side.
Rs. 80 (usd 1.1)
8/10

Mutton Peas Pulav 
Made three days a week, this is a pulao that is moist, gentle and aromatic. The aroma of the whole spices is what one tastes on the palate alongside the faint warmth of green chillies whose heat has been toned down by some coconut milk that goes into the pulao just before it is placed on dum. The meat in the pulao is soft and has a bit of fat ribboned through it, the peas are endearing in their soft bite.
Rs. 200 (usd 2.8)
8.5/10

Gourmet On The Road,
Food Lovers TV

popular breakfast spot 50 kilometres from bangalore, village eatery, bengaluru, rural bengaluru, nani hotel, masala dosa, dose, idli, vada, bisi bele bhath, chitranna, tomato rice, masala vade, kesari bath, coffee

Given its modest beginnings as a village eatery in a hut six or seven decades ago in Vijayapura, S. Narayan Rao, the late founder of Nani Hotel may have found it hard to fathom its current immense following that draws Bangaloreans to drive 50 kilometres for breakfast here. Having discovered its tiffin delights on a motorcycle ride a couple of months ago, I returned to savour breakfast, catch up with the owning family and patrons to find out what’s special here, including their much-loved Nani Hotel Masala Dosa. Hope you enjoy this episode, take care, stay safe and happy eating!

Tuppa Masala Dosa
The ghee masala dosa is the top draw with patrons here. Smeared with a spicy chutney as it roasts, the dosa is ladled with a dollop of potato palya and a top-up lashing of ghee to ensure the tuppa is what customers taste in plenty. The result is a golden-brown dosae that is slightly thick and biscuity in its crunch and lush with ghee, cradling within its fold a creamy, flavourful palya. The chutney makes for a spicy accompaniment.

Title: Tasting A Delicious, Traditional Kerala Meal | KAPPA CHAKKA KANDHARI | Ramassery Idli, Appam & Stew
Description:
#traditional #keralacuisine #bangalore

best kerala restaurant, bangalore, bengaluru, koramangala, traditional, malayali food, kappa chakka kandhari, appam and stew, karimeen, pearlspot fry, kappa fish curry, pazham kanji, pidi kozhi curry, duck roast, kappa vada, tapioca, ramassery idli, appam and stew, puttu, mutton coconut fry, meen pollichathu, tender coconut pudding, kandhari ice cream, payasam, chef regi mathew

The folks behind Kappa Chakka Kandhari restaurant take their food rather seriously, after all their menu is a showcase of Malayali fare based on their collective memories of growing up in Kerala. And spearheading this unique ‘nostalgic’ culinary initiative is Chef Regi Mathew, who has spent more than a decade extensively touring his home state, exploring recipes and connecting with cooks across homes, community kitchens, and even toddy shops. The resulting food is a labour of love, with ingredients sourced from micro-regions in Kerala to match the provenance of the dish, for instance the rice for the fabled Ramassery Idli comes from Palakkad, the home of the idli, the karimeen (pearl spot fish) from Vaikom, Kottayam, and so on… This fastidious approach to sourcing also seems to extend to the kitchen hands at KCK too, who hail from traditional kitchens and homes in ‘God’s own country’. In this episode, I partake of a lavish lunch that spans across a dozen preparations, made possible by their innovative menu approach that allows for diners to savour a string of delicacies in the course of a meal. Hope you enjoy this one, take care, stay safe and happy eating!

Note:
The set menus at Kappa Chakka Kandhari are priced upwards of Rs. 475 (usd 6.5) and in addition to a tasting of seven preparations, include a beverage and dessert too. Additional add-ons (limited servings), kappa vada, koorka fry, ramassery idli with chicken curry, are priced at Rs. 100 (usd 1.4) per dish.  

Rajayogi Meal
A set menu that’s fit for a king, this smorgasbord of a dozen dishes is sheer indulgence! Begin with juicy prawns in a coconut-kokum masala that is steamed in a petite banana leaf pouch, spicy ‘touchings’ of needle fish, the plumpest soft shell crabs, and a delicately flavoured pearl spot fish draped in a robust, toddy shop masala, amongst other delicacies that include a peppery chicken peralan and a slow-cooked mutton coconut fry. Description:
#pizza #yelahanka #bangalore

best pizzas, north bangalore, bengaluru, siddys pizza, pizza recipe, pizza, pizzeria, margherita, smoked chicken, garlic bread, pepperoni, handmade pizzas, italian, authentic sicilian style pizzas, siddy, siddhanth sawkar, yelahanka, bangalore

When Siddhanth Sawkar was forced to close his café and home catering-turned-food truck brand, Spitfire Barbeque, owing to the pandemic, he spent a couple of months mulling his next move, making pizzas. Not just a generic version as dished out by fast food chains! Instead, he dug deep into his experience as a culinary student in Southern Italy, to open a pizzeria serving Sicilian style pizzas in his erstwhile North Bengaluru café in Yelahanka New Town. Siddy’s Pizza, as I discovered during a leisurely visit, is a one-man passion enterprise, where Siddy, as Siddhanth is known, does everything from taking the order to putting together the pizzas to serving customers who quite often chat with him as the cheese-laden flavourful pies bake in the oven. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care, stay safe and happy eating!

Garlic Butter Bread
Pillowy soft and gushing with garlic-infused buttery flavour; the butter is molten as the bread comes out of the oven! Changes your perspective of what simple garlic bread can be! The cheddar cheese dip makes for an indulgent accompaniment.
Rs. 140 (usd 1.9)
9/10

Classic Margherita & Cheese - Large
Its dough fermented for a few hours, the pizza is firm and toasty, drooping at the edge, burdened under the weight of a generous topping of cheese. The sharp, spicy notes of the homemade tomato sauce, salsa semplice, is softened by the mozzarella. 
Rs. 350 (usd 4.8)
8/10

Smoked Chicken & Cheese - Large
The juicy personality of the chunky, smoked chicken franks take over the palate the moment you bite into this cracker of a pizza, followed then by the slightly, sweet crunch of the onions. The cheese and tomato sauce play second fiddle to the meat and onions. If you love smoked chicken, this pie is a must-have!
Rs. 420 (usd 5.8)
10/10

Classic Pepperoni & Cheese - Large
Lush in virgin olive oil, this is a classic Sicilian style pizza, its ‘bready’ texture quite similar to a focaccia. There’s plenty of mozzarella that sits atop the pizza, followed by the spicy sauce and onions. But it is the fat-laden savoury fervour of the pepperoni that is the hero of this pizza! This pizza is also the sort that would make for a great midnight snack when left over in the refrigerator.
Rs. 650 (usd 9)
9/10

Title: This Couple Serves The Authentic Taste Of Nellore | CHEPALA PULUSU | VIJAY KITCHEN | Andhra Bhojanam
Description:
#nellore #andhrafood #bangalore

nellore andhra restaurant, vijay kitchen, brookefield, whitefield, bengaluru, andhra meals, fish curry, chepala pulusu, fish fry, vegetarian bhojanam, rr chilli chicken, mutton pepper ghee roast, biryani, chicken fry biryani, nellore, small business

With a culinary lineage that goes back to Hotel Manju, supposedly the first table-service restaurant in Nellore, Andhra Pradesh in the sixties, Sashidhar Reddy and his wife, Vijayalakshmi, moved to Bengaluru from Nellore little over a year ago to open Vijay Kitchen, to serve dishes made to traditional family recipes. I visited this modest eatery set in the ground floor of their home in the suburb of Brookefield, where I not only savoured a delicious Andhra Bhojanam but also caught the making of an iconic Nellore Chepala Pulusu, a sour and spicy fish curry. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care, stay safe and happy eating. 

Plate Rice Meals
Served on a banana leaf tray, the rice meals is a simple but satisfying affair that consists of two vegetables, one dry and the other moist, a sambar, rasam and a nourishingly tasty pappu to keep company with the anam (steamed rice) and flavoured rice. There is also a sweet to round off the meal.
Rs. 99 (usd 1.4)
8/10 

Chepala Pulusu (Sour and Spicy Fish Curry)
Made by his wife, Vijayalakshmi, to a recipe that goes back to Sasidhar Reddy’s grandmother, the Chepala Pulusu is a must-try here. A sour and spicy affair, the fish curry is made the evening before, thereby allowing for the fish to soak up the vivacious character of the tamarind, raw mangoes, chilli powder and the secret fenugreek spice blend. 
Rs. 180 (usd 2.5)
10/10

Mamdikaya Royyalu (Mango Prawns)
A tangy preparation that juxtaposes fresh flavours of shrimp to the tart fervour of raw mangoes. Taste it with the annam (rice) to tone down some of its tangy flavours.
Rs. 250 (usd 3.4)
9/10

Chepala Fry (Fish Fry)
Chinese pomfret or lake pomfret naped in a pleasant masala; the skin is fried to a crisp.
Rs. 150 (usd 1.4)
7/10
 
Royyalu Avakkai
A spicy, homemade prawn pickle that makes for a great combination with steaming hot rice.
8/10
 
Mutton Pepper Ghee Roast 
The meat is moist and juicy, coated with coarsely ground pepper and tossed in the buttery lushness of ghee. The meat is cooked twice, first a roasted fry with masala, and then tossed around in hot ghee. 
Rs. 250 (usd 3.4)
9/10

RR Chilli Chicken
This dish should come with a ‘chilli hotness’ warning! Not for the faint-hearted, there is little else in this dish other than the chicken and tonnes of green chilli. The result is a unique taste that’s fiery at first but also the sort that endears itself once you get past the ‘suffering’! If you like it toned down, tell them so and they will toss it in some ghee.
Rs. 150 (usd 1.4)
8/10

Chicken Fry Biryani
A dish that was introduced as a means to consume leftover biryani rice, topped with chicken fry, the chicken fry biryani today is more popular than the Nellore biryani here. One can taste the warming flavours of the biryani spices in the kushka, the rice, that makes for a great combination with the robust tomato-onion rich masala of the chicken fry. 
Rs. 180 (usd 2.5)
8.5/10

Kripal Amanna,
Gourmet On The Road,

Note: This is a family run enterprise that is doing its best to cope with the realities of the new normal. The food is great, and the family does its best in its service assisted by a few staff members.
